lab.title: Create the first HTTP clock-in boundary
lab.objective: Create an ASP.NET Core composition root.
lab.task: Expose POST /clock-entries/clock-in over AsyncClockEntryService and return BadRequest, Conflict, or Created deliberately.
lab.startingCondition: Session 32 verified the database query boundary. Session 33 explicitly creates the previously nonexistent Web project, request/response contracts, controller, route, and async service call.

steps.text: Step 1/12: Create src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web.csproj with Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web, targeting net10.0 and referencing Domain and Infrastructure.
Step 2/12: Add the Web project to PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln.
Step 3/12: In Web/Requests, create sealed record ClockInRequest(int EmployeeId, DateTime ClockInTime).
Step 4/12: In Web/Responses, create sealed record ClockEntryResponse(int EmployeeId, DateTime ClockInTime).
Step 5/12: In Web/Controllers, create sealed ClockEntriesController : ControllerBase with ApiController and Route("clock-entries") attributes.
Step 6/12: Inject AsyncClockEntryService through the controller constructor.
Step 7/12: Add HttpPost("clock-in") action ClockInAsync returning Task<ActionResult<ClockEntryResponse>> and accepting ClockInRequest plus CancellationToken.
Step 8/12: Inside ClockInAsync, return BadRequest when EmployeeId is not positive. This is an expected request rejection, not an exception.
Step 9/12: Await TryClockInAsync and forward the CancellationToken. Return Conflict when the service reports an existing open entry.
Step 10/12: Return Created with ClockEntryResponse when persistence succeeds.
Step 11/12: In Web/Program.cs, add controllers, register persistence, ensure the SQLite database exists, and map controllers.
Step 12/12: Build Web, start it long enough to verify startup, then build the solution and run every test with --no-build.

reveals.title: Solution
reveals.text: The completed action validates input, awaits the service, and translates each expected result.
